contract_plain_english: The unrestricted printed claim has a genuine existence obstruction. A standard Cauchy random variable has infinite positive and negative tail integrals, so its Lebesgue expectation is undefined and the displayed right-hand side is infinity minus infinity. Symmetric principal-value cancellation does not rescue the book's literal formula because the book defines expectation as a Lebesgue integral and prints two separate one-sided integrals. The source does not name Cauchy; it is the canonical witness exposing the missing qualification.

source_evidence.anchor: valid for any random variable X (not necessarily non-negative)
source_evidence.observation: The universal wording includes random variables with two-sided heavy tails; the source states no expectation-existence hypothesis.

source_evidence.anchor: E X = integral_0^infinity P{X>t} dt - integral_-infinity^0 P{X<t} dt
source_evidence.observation: The right-hand side is written as the difference of two separate one-sided nonnegative integrals.

source_evidence.anchor: the expectation E X of a random variable X on a probability space (Omega, Sigma, P) is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral
source_evidence.observation: A signed expectation is governed by Lebesgue integration, not by an unstated symmetric principal-value convention.

source_evidence.anchor: The two sides of this identity are either finite or infinite simultaneously.
source_evidence.observation: Each nonnegative positive-part or negative-part tail integral may legitimately equal positive infinity.

binders: A probability space supporting a real-valued random variable X (PDF page 1; printed page 5; footnote 1).

An explicit two-sided heavy-tailed witness, for example a standard Cauchy random variable; the source itself does not name this witness, but its universal quantifier in Exercise 1.2.2 includes it (PDF page 3; printed page 7).
conclusions: For the Cauchy witness, integral from 0 to infinity of P{X > t} dt is positive infinity and integral from minus infinity to 0 of P{X < t} dt is positive infinity.
Consequently, both positive and negative parts of X have infinite expectation, so E X is undefined as the Lebesgue integral specified by the source (PDF page 1; printed page 5; footnote 1).

The printed right-hand side becomes positive infinity minus positive infinity, which is undefined; therefore the formula cannot be a meaningful equality for every random variable as literally claimed (PDF page 3; printed page 7; Exercise 1.2.2).

Symmetric Cauchy principal-value truncations may cancel to zero for the symmetric witness, but that value is neither the Lebesgue expectation nor the difference of the two separately displayed one-sided integrals.
definitions_and_conventions: A standard Cauchy witness may be specified by F_X(t) = 1/2 + arctan(t)/pi; then P{X > t} = 1/2 - arctan(t)/pi for t >= 0, and symmetry gives the corresponding lower tail.
The two displayed tail integrals are nonnegative extended integrals considered separately, as indicated by the layout of Exercise 1.2.2 (PDF page 3; printed page 7).

Lebesgue expectation of a signed random variable is undefined when both its positive-part and negative-part integrals are infinite, consistently with the source's identification of expectation with the Lebesgue integral (PDF page 1; printed page 5; footnote 1).
A Cauchy principal value would instead impose a linked symmetric truncation on the two sides; no such convention appears in Exercise 1.2.2 (PDF page 3; printed page 7).
hypotheses: Choose X with the standard Cauchy law, equivalently with symmetric tails of order 1/t; this is a mathematical witness to test the source's unrestricted phrase 'any random variable,' not an example printed in the source (PDF page 3; printed page 7; Exercise 1.2.2).
implicit_context: The obstruction concerns existence and interpretation of the two infinite integrals, not the algebraic sign or limits in the printed formula (PDF page 3; printed page 7; Exercise 1.2.2).

The source's preceding nonnegative lemma allows infinite tail integrals, so one cannot silently infer finiteness of either term in the generalized signed formula (PDF page 3; printed page 7; Lemma 1.2.1).
The Cauchy witness is diagnostic mathematical context forced by the universal claim; it is not additional content stated in the cited book pages.

details: The source's words 'any random variable' include distributions for which both one-sided first moments diverge (PDF page 3; printed page 7; Exercise 1.2.2).
A standard Cauchy variable supplies the canonical symmetric instance: both displayed nonnegative tail integrals diverge, leaving an undefined difference.
The book defines expectation as a Lebesgue integral (PDF page 1; printed page 5; footnote 1).

A symmetric principal value, even when finite, does not establish existence of that Lebesgue integral and is not licensed by the two separate improper integrals printed in Exercise 1.2.2 (PDF page 3; printed page 7).
The tail decomposition itself is correct when the signed expectation exists.

The obstruction is specifically the missing condition preventing simultaneous divergence of the positive and negative tail integrals; it does not refute the corrected integrable or one-sided-extended versions.

undebatable_constraints: The obstruction must address the source's literal universal quantifier, not replace it silently with an integrable-random-variable hypothesis (PDF page 3; printed page 7; Exercise 1.2.2).
The witness must make both displayed one-sided tail integrals infinite, so that the source's subtraction is genuinely of the form infinity minus infinity.

The conclusion must distinguish an undefined Lebesgue expectation from a finite symmetric principal value, because the source defines expectation as a Lebesgue integral (PDF page 1; printed page 5; footnote 1).
The source does not itself mention the Cauchy distribution, so the witness must be identified as a mathematical diagnosis of the printed claim rather than quoted source content.
The obstruction does not invalidate the identity for integrable X or whenever exactly one side is infinite and the extended Lebesgue expectation is defined.
